{{Short description|Concept in mathematics}}
In mathematics, the concept of a '''residuated mapping''' arises in the theory of [[partially ordered set]]s. It refines the concept of a [[monotonic function|monotone function]].

If ''A'', ''B'' are [[Partially ordered sets|posets]], a function ''f'': ''A'' → ''B'' is defined to be monotone if it is order-preserving: that is, if ''x''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''y'' implies ''f''(''x'')&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''f''(''y''). This is equivalent to the condition that the [[preimage]] under ''f'' of every [[down-set]] of ''B'' is a down-set of ''A''. We define a [[principal down-set]] to be one of the form ↓{''b''} = { ''b''<nowiki>'</nowiki> ∈ ''B'' : ''b''<nowiki>'</nowiki> ≤ ''b'' }. In general the preimage under ''f'' of a principal down-set need not be a principal down-set. If all of them are, ''f'' is called '''residuated'''.

The notion of a residuated map can be generalized to a [[binary operator]] (or any higher [[arity]]) via component-wise residuation. This approach gives rise to notions of left and right division in a partially ordered [[magma (algebra)|magma]], additionally endowing it with a [[quasigroup]] structure. (One speaks only of residuated algebra for higher arities). A binary (or higher arity) residuated map is usually ''not'' residuated as a unary map.<ref>Denecke, p. 95; Galatos, p. 148</ref>

==Definition==
If ''A'', ''B'' are posets, a function ''f'': ''A'' → ''B'' is '''residuated''' if and only if the preimage under ''f'' of every principal down-set of ''B'' is a principal down-set of ''A''.

==Consequences==
If ''B'' is a poset, the set of functions ''A'' → ''B'' can be ordered by the [[pointwise order]] ''f'' ≤ ''g'' ↔ (∀''x'' ∈ A) ''f''(''x'') ≤ ''g''(''x'').

It can be shown that a monotone function ''f'' is residuated if and only if there exists a (necessarily unique) monotone function ''f''<sup>&nbsp;+</sup>: ''B'' → ''A'' such that ''f''&nbsp;<small>o</small>&nbsp;''f''<sup>&nbsp;+</sup> ≤ id<sub>B</sub> and ''f''<sup>&nbsp;+</sup>&nbsp;<small>o</small>&nbsp;''f'' ≥ id<sub>A</sub>, where id is the [[identity function]]. The function ''f''<sup>&nbsp;+</sup> is the '''residual''' of ''f''. A residuated function and its residual form a [[Galois connection]] under the (more recent) monotone definition of that concept, and for every (monotone) Galois connection the lower adjoint is residuated with the residual being the upper adjoint.<ref>Erné, Proposition 4</ref> Therefore, the notions of monotone Galois connection and residuated mapping essentially coincide.

Additionally, we have ''f''<sup>&nbsp;-1</sup>(↓{''b''}) = ↓{''f''<sup>&nbsp;+</sup>(''b'')}. <!-- we need a more complete characterization -->

If ''B''° denotes the [[Duality (order theory)|dual order]] (opposite poset) to ''B'' then ''f'' : ''A'' → ''B'' is a residuated mapping if and only if there exists an ''f''<sup>&nbsp;*</sup> such that ''f'' : ''A'' → ''B''° and ''f''<sup>&nbsp;*</sup>: ''B''° → ''A'' form a [[Galois connection]] under the original [[antitone]] definition of this notion.

If ''f'' : ''A'' → ''B'' and ''g'' : ''B'' → ''C'' are residuated mappings, then so is the [[function composition]] ''gf'' : ''A'' → ''C'', with residual (''gf'')<sup>&nbsp;+</sup> = ''f''<sup>&nbsp;+</sup>''g''<sup>&nbsp;+</sup>. The antitone Galois connections do not share this property.

The set of monotone transformations (functions) over a poset is an [[ordered monoid]] with the pointwise order, and so is the set of residuated transformations.<ref>Blyth, 2005, p. 193</ref>

==Examples==
* The [[ceiling function]] <math>x \mapsto \lceil x \rceil </math> from '''R''' to '''Z''' (with the usual order in each case) is residuated, with residual mapping the natural embedding of '''Z''' into '''R'''.
* The embedding of '''Z''' into '''R''' is also residuated.  Its residual is the [[floor function]] <math>x \mapsto \lfloor x \rfloor</math>.

== Residuated binary operators ==
If • : ''P'' × ''Q''  → ''R'' is a binary map and ''P'', ''Q'', and ''R'' are posets, then one may define residuation component-wise for the left and right translations, i.e. multiplication by a fixed element. For an element ''x'' in ''P'' define ''<sub>x</sub>λ''(''y'') = ''x'' • ''y'', and for ''x'' in ''Q'' define ''λ<sub>x</sub>''(''y'') = ''y''  • ''x''. Then • is said to be residuated if and only if ''<sub>x</sub>λ'' and ''λ<sub>x</sub>'' are residuated for all ''x'' (in ''P'' and respectively ''Q''). Left (and respectively right) division are defined by taking the residuals of the left (and respectively right) translations: ''x''\''y'' = (''<sub>x</sub>λ'')<sup>+</sup>(''y'') and ''x''/''y'' = (''λ<sub>x</sub>'')<sup>+</sup>(''y'')

For example, every [[ordered group]] is residuated, and the division defined by the above coincides with notion of [[Group (mathematics)#Division|division in a group]]. A less trivial example is the set Mat<sub>''n''</sub>('''''B''''') of [[square matrices]] over a [[Boolean algebra (structure)|boolean algebra]] '''''B''''', where the matrices are ordered [[pointwise]]. The pointwise order endows Mat<sub>''n''</sub>('''''B''''') with pointwise meets, joins and complements. [[Matrix multiplication]] is defined in the usual manner with the "product" being a meet, and the "sum" a join. It can be shown<ref>Blyth, p. 198</ref> that {{math|1=''X''\''Y'' = (''Y''<sup> t</sup>''X'' &prime;)&prime;}} and {{math|1=''X''/''Y'' = (''X'' &prime;''Y''<sup> t</sup>)&prime;}}, where ''X &prime;'' is the complement of ''X'', and ''Y'' <sup>t</sup> is the [[transposed matrix]]).
